public_notes.title: Homelands Before Reservation Boundaries
public_notes.text: The Tribe's history places Mouache homelands along the eastern Rocky Mountains, from the Denver area south into New Mexico. It places Caputa homelands south of the Conejos River and in the San Luis Valley near the Rio Grande's headwaters. These are histories of the two bands that make up the Southern Ute Indian Tribe, not a map of present-day ownership or jurisdiction.

public_notes.title: Allotment And Different Paths
public_notes.text: The Tribe recounts that the 1895 Hunter Act opened the Ute Strip to allotment, homesteading and sales to non-Indians. Its history describes Mouache and Caputa families taking individual allotments, while Weenuchiu people opposed individual landholding and moved west. Its chronology dates Southern Ute allotment distribution to 1896. The accounts explain different paths among related Ute communities; they do not make today's governments interchangeable.

public_notes.title: Restoration And Future Generations
public_notes.text: Land loss is only part of this history. The Tribe's chronology records a Restoration Act returning land to the Southern Utes in 1937. It also records a 1984 Tribal Council resolution that made education a priority through a higher-education scholarship committee and program. These are historical milestones, not statements of today's land title, program funding or eligibility.

public_notes.title: Land And Restoration
public_notes.text: The Tribe's land-restoration account traces the Uncompahgre Reservation to an 1880 Act of Congress and an 1882 Executive Order. It describes pressure from livestock grazing and later energy development, and explains why the Tribe contests federal control of those lands. This is the Tribe's historical account and legal position, not an independent ruling on title or a current case update.

public_notes.title: Water And Self-Determination
public_notes.text: A July 10, 2025 Tribal statement links its defense of irrigation water to the 1923 Cedarview Decree. It reports that a July 8, 2025 court report and recommendation favored the Tribe in a water-diversion case. The statement connects this work to water for Tribal ranchers and farmers. It does not establish a final judgment or the case's current status.
